newsitem.title: HONG KONG: First Pacific sees better 97 on spinoffs.
newsitem.headline: First Pacific sees better 97 on spinoffs.

text.p: First Pacific Co Ltd, which posted a 20.5 percent drop in net profit for 1996, sees better results for 1997 if spinoffs of its overseas units go ahead as planned, managing director Manuel Pangilinan said on Monday.
The company is planning to list two of its Philippine units, Smart Communications in June or July this year and Fort Bonifacio Development Corp during the year, he said.

"If the Smart initial public offering (IPO) were to proceed in 1997, I think that would give rise to a fairly significant exceptional gain...equally, the possibility of Fort Bonifacio itself going into IPO," Pangilinan told a news conference.

Smart Communications is the company's major mobile phone operations in the Philippines held by First Pacific's Philippines flagship Metro Pacific Corp, while Fort Bonifacio is involved in developing the former Fort Bonifacio military facility in Metro Manila into an upmarket metropolis.
Market conditions, however, would decide whether the spinoffs would go ahead, Pangilinan said.
The blue chip conglomerate posted a 20.5 percent drop at the net profit level to US$204.2 million (HK$1.59 billion) for 1996 from US$257 million in 1995.

Executive director Thomas Yasuda also admitted that the company's telecommuniations subscriber base in Hong Kong had not grown much in 1996 due to increased competition and a focus on changing its customer network from an analog to digital one.

"We felt that 1996 would be a good year to pause and invest in the network," Yasuda said, adding the entry of new and competitive operators into the personal communications system market also caused an overall fall in prices.
He also added that in Hong Kong, the average revenue per user was likely to move lower to HK$500 per month by end 1997 from just under HK$600 per month currently.
"It would probably stabilise in 1999 to range between HK$350 and HK$400," Yasuda said, but added that such levels were still good compared with mature markets such as the United States.
